findings.title: Unpinned package executed on every start: cito-mcp
findings.detail: 'cito-mcp' launches cito-mcp through npx without a version. The client resolves the version at start time, so any future publish to that package name runs with your credentials. This is how postmark-mcp (Sept 2025) reached roughly 300 organisations.
findings.remediation: Pin an exact version and an integrity hash: "args": ["cito-mcp@<version>"] and drop the -y flag. Re-pin deliberately, after reviewing the diff.

findings.title: Description reads as instructions to the model (p=1.00): create_webhook
findings.detail: The description of 'cito-mcp.create_webhook' scores 1.00 on the instruction-detection model, and carries intent signals: credentials+fs_targets. Descriptions are documentation for a human, but they are delivered to the model as trusted context, so text that tells the model what to do is an attack surface rather than a description. The score is driven mainly by: cross_tool, fs_targets, entropy, log_len.

evidence.description: Create a webhook on this account: Cito starts POSTing the chosen events to the URL. Needs Pro or Scale; a plan error includes the upgrade link to relay. The URL must be public. The account owner is emailed. webhook.secret comes back ONCE: have the user store it in an environment variable such as CITO_WEBHOOK_SECRET, and do not repeat it in chat. Then call test_webhook. API calls: 1.

findings.remediation: Read the description against what the tool actually does. If the text is legitimate, it usually means the tool should not have to instruct the model at all - move the guidance into the parameter descriptions or the server's own docs.

evidence.description: Send a test to a webhook now and report what happened: status, statusCode, latencyMs and a plain-English diagnosis to relay. With event, sends a real recent sample of that event, signed and marked as a test (test: true, data.test: true, X-Cito-Test: true); without it, a short ping. API calls: 1.

findings.remediation: Read the description against what the tool actually does. If the text is legitimate, it usually means the tool should not have to instruct the model at all - move the guidance into the parameter descriptions or the server's own docs.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'cito-mcp': reads credentials or secrets + sends data outbound
findings.detail: 42 combination(s) exist where one tool reads credentials or secrets and another sends data outbound. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they reads credentials and can send data to an address it controls. A single prompt is enough to turn 'summarise this config' into a credential leak. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.detail: 10 combination(s) exist where one tool reads environment variables and another sends data outbound. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.

findings.title: No baseline supplied - drift detection is disabled
findings.detail: Without an approved snapshot the scanner cannot tell a tool that has always been there from one that appeared yesterday. The single most effective MCP control is the diff, and it needs a baseline to diff against.
findings.remediation: Run 'mcp-scrutiny baseline --config <file> --out mcp-baseline.json', commit the file, and pass it back with --baseline on every later scan.
